_readme: DECLARED COUNTS (checked by test/corpus_independence_test.dart, which reads them from tools/ai_accuracy.py --corpus and fails if they go stale): 53 cases over 38 distinct dish families; 33 distinct dish CLASSES; 48 coverage classes; top-4 classes hold 26%. ROADMAP M1 bar = 20 MEALS = 20 distinct dish classes. MET at 33, with thirteen classes spare. EVERY DECLARED CLASS HAS A CASE.
Labelled truth for tools/ai_accuracy.py.
Batch 1: 5 openly licensed, human-reviewed Indian meals plus the 1 original in-repo photo and 1 out-of-scope probe.
RoADMAP M1 asks for 20. We are not there yet, and the count is not
the thing being optimised - a corpus of 5 photos of the same dish
would score beautifully and tell us nothing.
kcal values are IFCT-style REFERENCE figures for the visible portion,
not laboratory measurements. 'confidence' is my honest read of how
defensible the label is: a thali I can name item by item is 'high'; a
bowl that a scan could fairly call either kadhi or dal is 'medium'.
Anything I could not name honestly was deleted, not guessed at.
Batch 2 added 5 more openly licensed, human-reviewed meals, chosen for dish BREADTH: 8 of the 16 candidates were bhindi, exactly the trap batch 1 hit with chole bhature, so only one bhindi was taken.

Batch 3 added 5 more openly licensed, human-reviewed meals. THE TRAP, THIRD TIME: of 18 candidates 8 were masala dosa and 7 were idli, so only 5 distinct dishes were taken. THE HONEST LIMIT: because the queries were breakfast items, all five are South-Indian breakfast. That is a real bias in the corpus; batch 4 must target curries, eggs and non-breakfast home cooking before any overall score is quoted.

Batch 4 added 5 more human-reviewed, non-breakfast meals. THE TRAP, FOURTH TIME: of 20 candidates 14 were chana/chole/chole-bhature, because three search terms were chole-based. Three of the five kept are therefore the same legume family - recorded here rather than hidden. Batch 5 must search one dish at a time to escape it. Batch 4 also adds the corpus's only NON-VEGETARIAN case, which was a real gap: our users are not all vegetarian and nothing else tested that.
INDEPENDENCE (2026-09-28). "22 cases" is NOT 22 facts. Three dish families
repeat here, so their errors carry 3x the weight of a family that appears once:
dal x3 (thali_ma08, chapati_dal_bhindi_plate, non_veg_thali),
chole x3 (north_indian_dinner, chole_papad_plate, chole_puri_halwa_thali),
sambar x2 (idli_sambar_chutney_plate, tamil_uthappam).
So: 22 cases over 17 DISTINCT dish families; 8 of 22 cases sit in a repeated
family; only 14 cases are the sole case of their family.
The bar in ROADMAP M1 is 20 MEALS = 20 distinct dishes. 17 < 20, so the bar is
NOT met, and any score quoted from this corpus must carry BOTH numbers.
Per-batch, the same way: batch 1 = 7 cases / 7 families; batch 2 (median 15.4%)
Producer: tools/ai_accuracy.py --corpus, which is the ONE definition of a
family; test/corpus_independence_test.dart executes it rather than re-deriving
it, and fails if these declared numbers stop matching the file.
"17 distinct families": 17 was the count of distinct dish NAMES at 22 cases.
Grouped by the judgement a scan actually has to make, that corpus was 13
distinct dish CLASSES - Dal / Dal Makhani / Urad Dal are one class,
Chole / Chana Masala one, Palak Paneer / Matar Paneer one, mutton / chicken /
dum biryani one - and dal, chole and sambar alone held 14 of its 22 cases.
BATCH 5 CLOSED PART OF THE GAP, from free photos and no model budget:
27 cases / 22 distinct dish names / 18 distinct dish CLASSES / 33 coverage
classes. New classes: khichdi, biryani, sarson da saag, aloo gobi, kofta.
The bar is 20 MEALS, so 18 of 20 - two classes short, from 13.
A third number, printed so the conservative one cannot be picked for me:
COVERAGE = 26 distinct classes across EVERY labelled item, because a thali holds
four judgements and class_of() only sees the first non-staple one.
22 cases / 17 names / 13 case-level classes / 26 coverage classes. The harness
prints all four and says which one the bar is judged on.
BATCH 5 (2026-09-28): 24 candidates fetched, 6 looked at, 5 ACCEPTED and
13 rejected with the reason recorded in photos.json. The batch was built
from the gap, not from what was easy: BATCH5_QUERIES is one query per
dish class the corpus lacked, and the fetcher grew a near-duplicate
check (64-bit dHash, Hamming <= 8) plus per-query and per-author caps
BEFORE fetching, because the fish-curry query offered five near-identical
files by one uploader. New classes: khichdi, biryani, sarson da saag,
aloo gobi, kofta. Two candidates were rejected for a truth I could not
name honestly, which is the rule working, not the rule being awkward.
BATCH 6 (2026-09-28): the last two classes the bar needed, chosen by GAP not
by convenience - one non-vegetarian class in 27 cases, no egg, no dessert,
no rice dish. BATCH6_QUERIES is one query per missing class. 8 candidates
fetched, 5 looked at, 3 ACCEPTED and 4 rejected with reasons, 1 declared
not-used because nobody looked at it.
NEW CLASSES: egg (egg bhurji), pulao (veg pulao + boondi raitha), kheer.
MEASURED: 30 cases / 25 distinct dish names / 21 distinct dish CLASSES / 35
coverage classes. The bar is 20 MEALS, so it is MET with one class spare,
and it is met honestly: egg bhurji and omelette are one class, mutton and
chicken biryani are one class, so a batch cannot buy the bar with synonyms.
BATCH 7 (2026-09-28): the SKEW, not the count. 13 of 30 cases were four
classes (dal x5, chole x4, paneer x2, sambar x2) = 43% of the corpus, so a
median over it is largely a median over dal and chole. Five classes were
targeted; Commons returned one usable photograph.
accepted 1  gajar halwa (a second dessert class; kheer was the only one)
rejected 3  a styled Bengali banana-leaf fish thali with three
unnameable items, an unidentifiable pale protein curry, and
a sweets-shop shot that repeats the halwa class
not_used 1  fetched, never looked at
So 21 -> 22 classes and the skew barely moved. Reported as it is: I am not
inflating a batch by accepting photographs I cannot label. The skew guard
pins the CURRENT concentration so it cannot worsen, and names <= 35% as the
target for a future batch instead of pretending it has been reached.
SKEW: 13 of 31 cases are four classes (dal x5, chole x4, paneer x2, sambar x2) = 42%. The bar is met, the SAMPLE is not yet even, and both facts belong in every number quoted from this corpus.
BATCH 8 (2026-09-28): FLATTEN, sized by arithmetic. The top 4 classes held
42% of 31 cases (dal x5, chole x4, paneer x2, sambar x2) and the readme
names <= 35% as the target, so the arithmetic is 13/(31+N): N=7 gives 35.1%,
N=8 gives 34.2%. BATCH8_QUERIES is therefore one query per class holding
exactly ONE case, and NONE of the four concentrated ones - a fifth dal makes
the median look better and the product no better. 18 queries, 94 candidates,
per-query and per-author caps plus the dHash near-dup check before fetching.
accepted 4  aloo gobi, baingan bharta, bhindi masala, dosa - every one a
class that had exactly one case, so all four flatten the skew
rejected 1  a plate of yellow rice and brown gravy filed as 'boryani'.
Not biryani: short uniformly yellow grain, no visible meat,
and the only other honest label is dal, which is a regression.
A photo that can only be labelled by guessing is not added
not_used 13  fetched, never looked at; declared not-used, not left
unreviewed, because an undecided photo is indistinguishable
from an accepted one
The dosa is the dose note: it is ROLLED, so the masala filling is not
visible and the label is Dosa rather than Masala Dosa. Same dish class
either way, so the count is unaffected - but the label says only what the
photograph shows.
BATCH 9 (2026-09-28): WIDEN, and the keys land WITH the photographs. Batch 8
flattened to 34%; the class count was 23 against a bar of 20, so count was
not the gap. The gap was that common home dishes had NO case at all: no
mushroom, capsicum, keema, french beans, sweet corn, jalebi or samosa, and
STAPLE_SIDES meant none could be smuggled in as a side. 7 queries, 24
candidates, per-query and per-author caps plus the dHash near-dup check.
accepted 2  keema (a new class), and a corn-capsicum masala scored as sweet
corn because corn is the dominant component
rejected 3  a Thai green curry with oyster mushrooms, not Indian; a plate
with french beans, rice, a bone-in lamb curry AND fried fish,
where class_of would take whichever I listed first; and a
sadya spread whose dominant component is a staple, so the
class would come from the fallback rather than a judgement
not_used 17  fetched, never looked at; declared not-used, not left
unreviewed
DISH_CLASS gains 8 new class keys IN THE SAME COMMIT as the photographs, with
their synonyms, because a key added after the fact is how a bar gets bought
with near-synonyms. Six of the eight have no case yet - the keys are there
so that when a photograph arrives it lands on ONE class, not a new one.
BATCH 10 (2026-09-28): the keys batch 9 opened, queried harder. Six of the
eight new class keys still had no case, and batch 9's own queries proved the
failure mode - an unsuffixed 'mushroom curry bowl' returned a THAI green
curry. So every query here carries 'indian' or 'home'. 6 queries, 21
candidates, per-query and per-author caps plus the dHash near-dup check.
accepted 2  jalebi with rabri, and a samosa with chutney - the two classes
batch 9 opened and left empty that Commons could fill cleanly
rejected 2  ON POLICY, NOT OPENED: a sixth DAL (dal is the worst single
class at 5) and a third PANEER (which would carry paneer past
chole into the top 4 and worsen the concentration). Both are
clean single-dish photographs, and both are thrown away
anyway: a good photo of a dish we already over-sample is
worth nothing to a median
rejected 1  a plate whose title alone names four non-staple components,
so class_of would score it by my typing order
not_used 16  fetched, never looked at; declared not-used
The two policy rejections are recorded as NOT LOOKED rather than as
judged-and-failed, because that is what happened - and because opening a
photograph only to reject it on a class count is a minute of the owner's
laptop spent on an outcome arithmetic has already decided.
BATCH 11 (2026-09-28): the six DECLARED class keys no case reached. The
target was measured, not chosen - test_the_dish_classes_are_distinct.py
prints DISH_CLASS keys the corpus never lands in: capsicum, french beans,
khakra, mushroom, raitha, uthappam. A declared key with no case is a promise
the corpus is not keeping, and it is the cheapest win there is: the class is
already a decision, so a photograph raises the count without inventing a
category, keeps every family at one case so independence does not worsen,
and lowers the concentration.
6 queries, 6 candidates, 3 downloaded after the caps and the dHash check
accepted 1  stuffed capsicum - the pepper is unambiguous; the filling is
recorded as what it looks like and NOT asserted as paneer,
because at that light rice and crumbled paneer are not
separable and guessing would be a false label
rejected 2  'uttpam and dal vada': the title claims uthappam but the pale
portion is vegetable rice, and the two certain items are vada
(already a class) and a staple chutney - so the class would be
decided by which reading I picked. Uthappam stays empty.
'different dinner nashik': the dominant item is garlic bread,
which is not an Indian class, so it would manufacture a new
UNDECLARED class through the fallback - the exact defect this
batch's own guard exists to catch
FIVE OF THE SIX TARGET CLASSES ARE STILL EMPTY - khakra, mushroom, raitha,
uthappam, french beans - and that is the result, not something to hide. Batch
7 recorded the same shape: six queries, one usable photograph. Commons is
thin on these dishes, and the honest next move is a second round with
regional spellings rather than loosening the cuisine constraint that batch 9
proved is what makes a query find the wrong cuisine.
BATCH 12 (2026-09-28): the five classes batch 11 left empty, queried by
REGIONAL SPELLING. Batch 11 got 1 usable photograph from 3 downloaded, so this
round changes the NAMES rather than adding more cuisine words: Commons is thin
on these dishes and thin in a particular way - the uploads are captioned in a
regional or transliterated form, not the dictionary form. Khakra -> khakro;
mushroom -> dhingra; raitha -> raita and potato raita; uthappam -> uttapam;
french beans -> gavar phali and beans poriyal. 10 queries, 18 candidates, 5
downloaded after the per-query and per-author caps and the dHash check.
accepted 3  uthappam x2 (its first two cases) and aloo raita (its first)
rejected 2  a botanical photograph of a guar plant in flower - not a dish,
and the lesson kept is that a botanical NAME finds a botanical
photograph, so a plant-named class needs a DISH word in the query
and a vegetable biryani that would be a THIRD biryani, with the
raita beside it a side dish. Putting raita first would have won
this batch the raitha class, but the class would then have been
decided by my typing order - the fault batch 10 rejected a
four-component plate for. A wanted class is not a reason to
reorder the truth
STILL EMPTY: khakra, mushroom and french beans. The regional-spelling strategy
worked for uthappam and raitha and did not work for the other three. The honest
reading is that Commons has very few photographs of a khakra, a mushroom masala
or a french-bean sabzi that are unambiguously those dishes. If there is a next
attempt it should change the DISH FORM - a whole thali rather than a close-up -
and if that is thin too, the right conclusion is that these three stay empty and
the bar is met without them.
BATCH 13 (2026-09-28): THE DISH-FORM ROUND, AND IT LEARNED NOTHING - WHICH IS NOT
THE SAME AS FINDING NOTHING. Khakra, mushroom and french beans were queried a third
way, by dish FORM (bowl, gravy, curry, sabzi) rather than by name, because batch 12's
own commit named that as the next move. Ten queries returned 0 candidates.
THAT ZERO WAS NOT A FINDING, and the control query is what proved it. A known-good
query that had returned results two batches earlier ALSO returned 0, and the API was
returning HTTP 429 - rate-limited - for every query. So the zero was a fact about US
(we were throttled) on its way into a case record as a fact about three DISHES
(Commons has no photograph of a khakra). Those are different claims and the first one
would have made three classes look permanently unfillable.
So nothing was recorded as a negative finding, and the three classes stay empty
PENDING a retry rather than declared unfillable. The fetcher no longer allows the
confusion: SEARCH_FAILURES records every query that was never asked, and main() exits
3 with the queries named instead of printing a candidate count. Guarded by
tools/ai_accuracy/test_a_throttled_fetch_is_not_a_zero.py, which includes the check
that stops the fix being its own bug - a genuine empty result set is still reportable,
because that is the case the rule exists to keep.
The principle was already in this repo's own tool and simply had not been applied
here: ai_accuracy.py carries the comment 'When the free model is rate-limited, that is
not a result'. It was written for model calls and the fetcher's search path was never
brought under it. This is the same lesson one code path over.
BATCH 14 (2026-09-28): THE QUERIES WERE THE PROBLEM, AND A CONTROL SAID SO. Batch
13 also returned zero, so three batches have now returned zero for three
DIFFERENT reasons and a control query is the only reason I know which is which:
CONTROL, known-good, worked in batch 12 ..... 1 candidate   <- the API is fine
'filetype:bitmap "mushroom curry" bowl gravy'  0         <- batch 13's wording
'filetype:bitmap "mushroom curry"' ........... 3         <- same dish, fewer words
'mushroom curry' (no filetype filter) ........ 3
'khakra gujarati' (no filetype filter) ....... 0         <- this one is thin
So batch 13's cause was MY query construction. filetype:bitmap plus a quoted
phrase plus two form words is over-constrained, and batch 13's premise - widen the
dish FORM - widened the query into uselessness. The dish was there the whole time.
8 queries, 19 candidates, 5 downloaded.
accepted 1  beans and potato in a steel bowl - a dry sabzi, not a gravy, with
visible potato cubes, a dried red chilli and cumin. French beans'
first case; the class has been declared and empty since batch 9
rejected 3  two OPENED, both because the pixels do not show the dish the title
promises: 'mushroom poori' is a street plate of onion, carrot,
chilli sauce and poori with NO MUSHROOM VISIBLE, and one is raw
green beans at market. One rejected on the filename WITHOUT being
opened - a Latin species binomial with a field-record suffix is a
botanical record - recorded as not-looked, not judged-and-failed
not_used 1  'curry chicken green beans' names two non-staple components, so the
class would be decided by my typing order; decidable from the title
MUSHROOM IS STILL EMPTY, and now for an honest reason rather than a throttle: the
dish is demonstrably on Commons - three candidates the moment the form words came
off - but what comes back is street food and botanical records rather than a plate
of mushroom curry. Only KHAKRA has now come back empty from every angle, which
makes it the one real candidate for a genuine absence.
BATCH 15 (2026-09-28): THE FIRST CONTROL-SUPPORTED NEGATIVE FINDING. 7 queries
with the CONTROL INSIDE THE SET rather than run separately, because a control run
minutes earlier is a claim about a moment that has passed. 3 downloaded, accepted
0, rejected 3.
CONTROL 'filetype:bitmap uthappam breakfast' .. returned hits, exit 0, so every
query in the set was asked
'filetype:bitmap khakra' ...................... 8 candidates, NONE food - a 1784
map of the Ganges, the Khakra
Math Palace, the Ghaghara river
'filetype:bitmap "khakra rotli"' ................ 0
'filetype:bitmap khakro' ........................ 0
'filetype:bitmap "gujarati khichdi"' ............ 0
The per-query cap was RAISED to 8 for that measurement, so a cap cannot masquerade
as an absence - the batch-15 run itself skipped candidates under the cap, and
without raising it I would have been reading my own cap as a fact about the food.
So khakra is not absent because the food is. It is absent because 'khakra' is a
proper noun that a 2026 map and a palace both match, and the dish needs a word
beside it that nobody has captioned. The honest reading is not 'khakra cannot be
photographed' but 'khakra cannot be SEARCHED with the words available' - and that
is a statement about searching, which is a different thing and a reversible one.
MUSHROOM REMAINS EMPTY for the fourth characterised reason: the dish is
demonstrably on Commons but photographed as a dosa plate or a street platter where
the mushroom cannot be identified. What a mushroom case needs is a photograph where
a mushroom is VISIBLE, and no query in three batches has produced one.
BATCH 16 (2026-09-28): THE LAST TWO EMPTY CLASSES, ATTACKED BY SYNONYM. Batch 15's
control-supported negative finding said khakra 'cannot be SEARCHED with the words
available', so this round stopped trying other spellings and used a DIFFERENT NAME
for the food: mathari, the bhakri it is eaten with, farsi puri, and dhingra (the
Hindi word for mushroom) plus the visible forms sabzi and fry - because a mushroom
case needs a photograph where a mushroom is VISIBLE. 7 queries with the control
first, 3 downloaded, accepted 1, rejected 2.
accepted 1  BUTTON MUSHROOM FRY - whole button mushrooms, stems and caps
unmistakable, lightly glazed with pepper. What batch 15 said the
class needed and three batches failed to find. MEDIUM confidence,
stated rather than buried: the mushrooms are certain, but the frame
carries no Indian marker - no masala, no onion, no rice, no roti. The
identification as an Indian preparation rests on 'mushroom fry'
being a standard Indian home dish, which is a claim about the
CAPTION and not about the picture, and the corpus's bar is Indian
meals, so that is recorded as what it is
rejected 2  'brig gen ashok dhingra exits a uh60 black hawk helicopter' - the
query was `dhingra`, the Hindi word for mushroom, and the search
returned a photograph of a BRIGADIER GENERAL NAMED ASHOK DHINGRA
getting out of a helicopter. The Hindi word for mushroom is also
an Indian SURNAME. A name search is not a dish search. And
'githunguri tea farm' - a tea plantation in Java, which is what
`mathari` returned
KHAKRA IS NOW EXHAUSTED AS A SEARCH PROBLEM, which is a different statement from
'khakra cannot be photographed': the word is a proper noun a map, a palace and a
river all match, and its synonyms reach a tea plantation in Java. Four names, four
non-dishes. The remaining honest options are a photograph from a human hand, or
accepting a corpus with 29 of its 33 declared classes filled - a decision, not a
failure, and not mine to take silently.
BATCH 17 (2026-09-28): KHAKRA, FOUND - AND A CORRECTION TO MY OWN CONCLUSION.
At the end of batch 16 this file said 'KHAKRA IS NOW EXHAUSTED AS A SEARCH
PROBLEM... Four names, four non-dishes.' Six queries had used four spellings of
one word in one search mechanism, and I generalised from that sample to the
population. The FIRST query of batch 17 - the double-k spelling, khakhra, which
no batch had tried - returned the dish.
That is this whole line of work's lesson applied to my own conclusion: a negative
finding needs a control, and 'I tried N things' is not a control, it is a sample.
5 queries with the control first, 2 downloaded, accepted 1, rejected 1.
accepted 1  KHAKHRA - broken shards of a thin crisp deep-golden fried disc with
ajwain, fried onion and a papery flake. Unmistakable, and nothing
else in the corpus resembles it. Khakra's first case; declared in
batch 9, empty through batches 10-16
rejected 1  'dhokla karachi' - a real Gujarati dish and NOT in DISH_CLASS, so
it would manufacture a new UNDECLARED class through the fallback.
Recorded as a CANDIDATE for a deliberate decision rather than added
on the strength of one photograph
AND A MECHANISM FINDING THAT WAS WRONG, RETRACTED 2026-09-28. I reported that
the category-scoped query was what found the khakhra, and that for a dish whose
name is a proper noun the right question is 'what is filed under the cuisine'.
`incategory:"Gujarati cuisine"` DOES NOT EXIST as a Commons category, verified
against the API. So `incategory:` with a non-existent category does not return
zero - it alters the search in a way I never established, and the Gujarati snacks
that query surfaced came from somewhere I cannot now account for.
WHAT ACTUALLY FOUND THE KHAKHRA was the double-k spelling on its own, with no
category in the query. That finding stands. This one does not, and it is
retracted in the record rather than deleted, because a published claim that is
then falsified is worth more than one never made. The guard that makes this
class visible is test_a_search_category_must_exist.py.
moving. Every declared class now has a case, so the class count cannot grow
honestly, and the note's own guidance applies: watch the concentration, not the
class count. 22 of 33 classes held exactly one case; the top four held 13 of 49,
which is 27%. Adding one case to each of EIGHT singleton classes would give 57
cases with the top four still at 13 - 23% - and dal and chole are never touched,
because growing the two largest classes is the regression batches 8 and 10 were
built to remove.
THE TRADE, STATED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: eight families become repeated, so
independence moves the other way - 20 of 49 becomes 24 of 53 here. Concentration
falls, independence falls, the sample gets bigger. A median over more cases in
more classes is a better instrument, and that is a trade rather than a free
improvement, which is why both numbers are reported together every time.
9 queries with the control first, 5 downloaded, accepted 4, rejected 1
accepted 4  idli in sambar (a steel bowl of about nine whole steamed idlis in
thick orange sambar with mustard seed; truth [Idli, Sambar] because
the plate is named for the idlis and the sambar is there)
medu vada (three craggy golden rings - a form nothing else in the
corpus has), jalebi (orange syrup-glossed coils), samosa (four
golden triangles with green coriander chutney)
rejected 1  'eierspeise im gasthaus' - the `egg curry` query returned an
AUSTRIAN dish. Eierspeise is scrambled egg and Gasthaus is a pub.
Batch 9's lesson in a form I had not anticipated: the cuisine
constraint has to survive TRANSLATION, not merely being English
YIELDED 4 OF THE 8 PLANNED. gajar halwa, kheer and pulao returned nothing that
survived the caps, so those classes are still singletons. Recorded, not hidden:
the concentration moves 27% -> 25%, not the 23% the arithmetic planned.
AND ONE MEASUREMENT THAT WOULD OTHERWISE BE A MYSTERY. Batch 18 added a case called
'idli_in_sambar_bowl' - nine whole idlis in thick sambar - and sambar went from 2 cases
to 3 while idli did not move at all. The reason is that `idli` is in STAPLE_SIDES, so
class_of() skipped it as a staple side and returned the next non-staple, which is
sambar. MEASURED, not inferred:
'idli' in STAPLE_SIDES  ->  True
class_of([Idli, Sambar])  ->  'sambar'
So the photograph is idli in sambar, and the class the corpus assigns is sambar. That is
the mapping working as designed rather than a bug, and it is recorded here because the
alternative is a reader finding sambar's count had moved and no explanation. Whether idli
ought to be a staple is arguable - it is a steamed rice cake, not an accompaniment - but
changing STAPLE_SIDES now would move the class count, and that is a decision with
consequences rather than a fix, so it is named here and not made quietly.
The batch therefore widened THREE of its four accepted cases into singleton classes as
planned - vada, jalebi and samosa each 1 -> 2 - and the fourth went to sambar, which was
already a repeated family. Concentration moved 27% -> 26% rather than the 23% the
eight-case arithmetic planned, because three of gajar halwa, kheer and pulao returned
nothing that survived the caps.
BATCH 19 (2026-09-28): LEARNED NOTHING, AND IT IS NOT A FINDING - FOR THE THIRD TIME
IN THREE DIFFERENT WAYS. Batch 18 named its own failures - gajar halwa, kheer and pulao
returned nothing that survived the caps - and batch 17 had proved that CATEGORY-SCOPED
search reaches food where text search reaches a map. So batch 19 retried those three the
way batch 17 found the khakhra.
8 queries, control first, and the result was: the control returned a candidate and EVERY
category-scoped query returned none.
AND THE CAUSE IS MY OWN AGAIN, so this is NOT a negative finding about the dishes. I
guessed the category NAMES. `incategory:"Indian sweets"` and `incategory:"Indian rice
dishes"` are my inventions - Commons does not use them, or uses longer forms - and an
instrument whose name is wrong returns zero in exactly the same shape as a dish that does
not exist. Batch 17's category worked because "Gujarati cuisine" happens to be a real
Commons category; these three are guesses wearing the same syntax.
SO THE THREE ZEROS IN THIS CORPUS NOW HAVE THREE DIFFERENT CAUSES, and only the third is
a fact about the food:
batch 13 ...... HTTP 429, every query refused        - a fact about OUR access
batch 13 retry  over-constrained wording             - a fact about MY query
batch 15 ...... khakra is a proper noun that a map, a palace and a river all match -
the first genuinely-supported negative finding
batch 19 ...... a CATEGORY NAME I invented           - a fact about MY instrument
The general form, and it is the fourth instance: every one of these was an instrument
failing in a way that produced the same output as the world being empty. The only reason
any of them was caught is that a CONTROL was in the query set - a query that could have
been positive and was. Without it, batch 19's zero would have become "Commons has no
photograph of kheer", and kheer is not a rare dish; it is one of the commonest in the
corpus's own coverage list.
WHAT A REAL ATTEMPT NEEDS, and I am not claiming it works: a category name READ OFF
COMMONS rather than invented, or a category lister, so the instrument is verified before
it is used to conclude anything. That is a small piece of tooling and it is the honest
next step - and until it exists, no category-scoped zero in this corpus means anything.

cases.note: In-repo original: one katori palak paneer + one roti.
OUT OF SCOPE on purpose. Chickpeas, avocado, tomato, cucumber, greens. No Indian dish is present; any Indian answer here is an invention.
Steel tray, shot from above. Unambiguous: a large portion of white rice, a yellow dal, a dry green sabzi, a brown curry, one empty compartment.
One steel bowl of dal makhani, near-overhead, cream streaks and cream visible. The single most identifiable Indian dish there is.
A white bowl of yellow kadhi seen from above, with a ghee and red-chilli temper garnish. 'Medium' because a scan could reasonably call this dal.

A yellow bowl of urad dal with two chapati on a plate, with raw onion rings, cucumber and lemon on the side. BATCH-1 CORRECTION: the first run scored onion and cucumber as INVENTED dishes. They are plainly in the photo - I described them in the note and then forgot to put them in the truth. The harness was right; my label was wrong.

Steel plate, overhead. A bowl of chole (chickpeas in gravy with green chilli), a dry spiced potato bhaji, two chapati, and a glass of tea. BATCH-1 CORRECTION: the first label said 'Chole, Dal, Roti' - there is NO dal in this photo, and the reference total was 200 kcal short, which is what produced the alarming 37.7% error. The model was closer to right than my label was. Corrected after looking at the image at full size.
White oval plate from above: a mound of white rice and bhindi masala (okra in a red gravy, coriander and green chilli).
One white plate, overhead: a mound of roasted mashed eggplant with visible seeds and green chilli. A single dish.
A steel bowl on a plain blue background, shot from above: pale green bottle-gourd cubes in a thin yellow-brown gravy.

A yellow bowl of matar paneer (paneer strips and green peas in an orange-red gravy). Loose peas and a block of paneer sit beside the bowl as styling, and are NOT labelled - a person photographing their lunch would log the bowl. That choice is why this case is 'medium'.

A square plate: two chapati, a chopped green bhindi sabzi and a yellow dal. NOTE: the file is named '...and_dal_rice' but there is NO rice in the photo - I labelled from the image, not the filename. There is also a small dark item at the plate edge I cannot identify, so it is left unlabelled rather than guessed.

A folded masala dosa on a steel plate with two small bowls of chutney, shot from above. 'Medium' because the filling inside the fold is not visible, so the potato-vs-onion split is a judgement call, and the two chutneys cannot be told apart.
A white plate from above: four steamed idli and two small bowls, one pale brown and one orange. Home-style, not styled.
Rava idli in a steel bowl on a home table, with sambar in a black bowl and two chutney bowls. Overhead and plainly home-cooked.

A single uthappam on a banana leaf with small bowls of sambar and chutney. Unmistakable and clearly a home serving. CORRECTION 2026-09-28: this case was previously reported as the worst failure - the model 'inventing' a dish. Measured live, the model answered "Vegetable Uttapam", which IS this dish; my alias list simply lacked that spelling. The model was right and my label was the bug. A false accusation is worse than no measurement because it sends you fixing the wrong thing.
On a banana leaf: two idli, one golden vada, a bowl of sambar and chutney, with a steel tumbler. 'Medium' because vada and boondi in the sambar can be confused at this size.
A white plate from above: chole in a small steel bowl with two papad triangles beside it. Clean, home-style, plainly identifiable.
A close overhead view of chana masala cooking in a pan, garnished with coriander. 'Medium' because there is no plate or bowl for scale, so the portion is an estimate.
A steel thali from above: chole, a puri, and a portion of gajar halwa. Three clearly separate items.
A white plate from above: kidney beans with brinjal pieces in a brown masala. 'Medium' because rajma-with-brinjal and plain rajma are a judgement call from the photo alone.

The corpus's only NON-VEGETARIAN case, which is a real gap: our users are not all vegetarian and nothing else tested that. The photographer's own Commons description is the ground truth here, and it lists MORE than I first labelled: 'plain rice, dal, rajma, fish with mustard, chicken curry, carrot and cucumber salad, pickle, green chili, papad, and kheer'. My first label named only four items, which would have scored real food as invented. Using the photographer's description rather than my eye, because on a crowded plate my eye is the weaker authority.

Gujarati khichuri on a steel-and-ceramic plate, from above: a bowl of khichdi, three khakra, one dry vegetable sabzi. The small steel katori of thin dal/sauce is NOT in the truth: I could not name it honestly, and a guess in the truth column is how an earlier baseline was wrong by 37.7%.

Home-cooked plate from above: a large plate of mutton biryani with mutton pieces and a whole potato, a small glass bowl of extra mutton gravy, and cucumber slices. The extra gravy bowl is counted inside the biryani figure, not as a second dish.
One steel bowl of sarson da saag and one makki di roti, shot from above. Countable, and the classic winter pairing - a dish class the corpus had no case for at all.
One white bowl of aloo gobi on a newspaper, close to above. A single-dish case, which the corpus barely had: most of its cases are thalis, so a one-bowl scan was never measured.
Twelve kofta in a red gravy on a square plate, from above. The count is deliberate: this is a COUNTING case as well as a naming one, and counting is where the app has been weakest.

A yellow compartment tray shot from above: egg bhurji with onion, tomato and coriander; three chapati; and a meat curry in two compartments. THE MEAT IS NOT IDENTIFIABLE from the photo, so the truth says 'Meat Curry' and every specific answer is an accepted alias - a model that says mutton when it is beef has not invented anything, and a truth column that demanded one answer would score it wrong for a reason that is not the model's fault. The 2nd meat compartment is counted once.

A white bowl of veg pulao on a floral plate beside a yellow bowl of boondi raitha, from above. The rice is WHITE, not yellow, so pulao vs plain rice with vegetables is a judgement - 'Rice' is therefore an accepted alias, and the label is medium confidence rather than a pretence of certainty.

One steel bowl of chahao kheer - purple rice pudding with milk - on a tablecloth, with a spoon. The corpus had NO dessert case at all, and a thali photograph routinely contains one: the only dessert in the corpus before this was gajar halwa, inside someone else's thali.

A glass bowl of gajar ka halwa with two cashews on top, on a blue plate, three tomato slices beside it, shot from above. One clearly readable dish plus a garnish - the shape of case the corpus barely had, and a second dessert class after kheer.

A shallow steel bowl on a plain white surface, shot from above: one dish of potato and cauliflower florets in an orange-brown masala, nothing else on the plate. Every item is nameable and the dish is unambiguous - aloo gobi is the only reading. A second case for the aloo gobi class, which had one.

A hammered steel bowl on a restaurant table, a spoon resting in a coarse mashed preparation with visible charred dark skin and chopped coriander on top. The roasted skin fragments are what make it baingan bharta rather than a tomato mash. Medium rather than high: it is a restaurant plate, not a home kitchen, and the mash is finer than a home-roasted bharta.

A white bowl full of okra cut length-wise, coated in a spiced onion-tomato masala, on a dark counter. Every pod is visibly okra and nothing else is in the bowl, so the judgement is single and clean. A second case for the bhindi class, which had one.

A white plate holding twelve round kofta in a red-orange oil gravy with a coriander garnish, filling the frame. One dish, one judgement, no second component. A second case for the kofta class, which had one.

A white oval dish of bone-in chicken pieces - two drumsticks and a thigh, the bone and skin clearly visible - in a dark brown onion-tomato masala with cracked spice and seeds. The protein is identifiable, so this is a clean single judgement. It is also a dish CLASS the corpus had no case for at all: chicken curry had appeared only as an item inside a thali, and a thali is scored as the thali.

A white plate of long-grain basmati with a distinct browned fried-onion layer on top, whole spice and a green chilli visible, and bone-in mutton pieces to the left. This is the evidence the rejected 'boryani' lacked: long distinct grain, a fried-onion cap, and visible bone-in meat. A second case for the biryani class, which had one.

A steel thali holding a rolled dosa, a compartment of white chutney and a compartment of orange gravy with visible vegetable pieces. The dosa is the dish. The filling is NOT visible because the dosa is rolled, so the label is Dosa and not Masala Dosa - saying 'masala' would be a claim about something inside. Both labels land on the same dish class. A second case for the dosa class, which had one.

A steel bowl of minced meat in a masala, with green peas, chopped coriander, ginger julienne and a tomato wedge on top. The mince is unmistakably keema, and the bowl holds one dish and nothing else. Keema is a NEW dish class: the corpus had no mince case at all, and it is a very common home dish.

A metal kadai of sweet corn kernels with red and green capsicum in a thick brown masala, shot close and slightly out of focus. Both vegetables are genuinely present, so the truth names both and the class lands on corn, which is the dominant component. Medium rather than high: the frame is soft, and a scan could reasonably call this capsicum-forward instead.

Two foil plates of coiled, syrup-glazed orange sweets beside four paper cups of thick white rabri topped with pistachio slivers, on a wooden street-food table. The spiral coil shape is jalebi and nothing else, and the cups are rabri. Jalebi is a class batch 9 opened and left empty; this is its first case.

One triangular fried samosa on a white plate with a mint chutney, a red sauce and a dark shredded accompaniment I could not name. The samosa is unambiguous; the chutney is a staple so class_of() skips it; the third accompaniment is not asserted because I could not identify it. Medium rather than high: it is a dim restaurant table, not the home plate the corpus mostly holds.

One whole green bell pepper on a white plate, stem and all, slit lengthwise and packed with a pale cooked filling in which corn kernels, diced carrot and green peas are individually visible, photographed in low light on a dark table. The pepper is unambiguous. The filling is a rice-and-vegetable mixture and I am not claiming paneer for it, because at this light I cannot tell whether the pale grains are rice or crumbled paneer - so the truth names the capsicum, which is what the class is decided on, and this note records what the filling looks like instead of guessing at it. Capsicum's first case; the class was declared and empty.

Three thick white savoury rice pancakes on a bright pink square plate, each roughly a hand across, with visible chopped onion, green chilli slices, diced tomato and coriander, browned and blistered in patches from the pan. A small glass bowl of pale speckled chutney sits at the top of the plate. The thick porous white batter with onion and chilli is uthappam and nothing else, and this is its first case in the corpus.

One large onion uthappam served on a green banana leaf on a stainless steel tray, the pancake pale and glossy with translucent onion, green chilli rings, coriander and turmeric-tinted fried patches across its surface. A red-orange pickle or chutney is partly visible at the lower left edge. A second, different photograph of the same dish is legitimate sampling rather than duplication: it tests whether the model is consistent on one dish across two photographs.

A shallow orange bowl of aloo raita: a pale pink-white yogurt base thick with visible cubes of boiled potato, chopped green chilli, roughly torn coriander leaves and a dusting of red chilli powder across the surface. A sliver of a white plate is visible at the top left corner. The potato cubes in a yogurt base make this potato raita rather than plain raita, and the class is the same either way. Raitha's first case.

A shallow steel bowl of a cooked dry beans preparation: chopped green beans cut short, visible cubes of boiled potato, one dried red chilli and cumin seeds. It is a dry sabzi rather than a gravy curry, and the photograph is a close view into the bowl on a stovetop. The beans are the dish and the potato is a second component, so class_of takes the beans. Medium rather than high because the photograph is a bowl being cooked rather than a plated serving, so there is no portion context. French beans' first case; the class has been declared and empty since batch 9.

Whole button mushrooms on a white plate, stems and caps unmistakable, lightly glazed and flecked with cracked pepper and a few fried spice fragments, with one loose fragment off to the side. This is what batch 15 said the class needed and three previous batches failed to find: a photograph where the mushroom is VISIBLE rather than hidden under a dosa or dissolved in a katori of gravy. MEDIUM confidence and the reason is stated rather than buried - the mushrooms are certain and the preparation is a dry fry, but the frame carries no Indian marker: no masala, no onion, no rice, no roti. The identification as an Indian preparation rests on 'mushroom fry' being a standard Indian home dish, which is a claim about the caption and not about the picture. The corpus's bar is Indian meals, so that is exactly what this is.

A white plate holding broken shards of a thin, crisp, deep-golden fried disc, with visible carom/ajwain seed, small fried onion pieces and one papery translucent flake, on a dark counter. The form, the fry colour, the ajwain and the onion are all characteristic of a Gujarati crispbread, which is khakhra, and nothing else in the corpus resembles it. Found by the DOUBLE-K SPELLING, which no earlier batch tried, after batch 16 recorded this class as an exhausted search problem - so the exhaustion was a fact about four spellings in one search mechanism, not about the food. Khakra's first case; declared in batch 9, empty through batches 10-16.

A steel bowl holding about nine whole steamed idlis - pale golden, porous, each with the grain and the slightly flattened disc shape - sitting in a thick orange sambar with visible mustard seed and a metal spoon resting in the bowl. Truth is [Idli, Sambar]: the plate is named for the idlis and the sambar is the accompaniment, and saying so is better than pretending the sambar is not there. Idli's second case.

Three golden-brown craggy ring-shaped fritters on a steel plate, each with the crinkled batter surface and the central hole of a medu vada. The form is distinctive and nothing else in the corpus resembles it. High confidence. Vada's second case.

A white plate piled with orange, glossy, syrup-soaked batter coiled into flat spirals, photographed close under warm light with the syrup sheen visible on every coil. Jalebi and nothing else. Jalebi's second case, and a different photograph from the rabri plate in batch 10 - which is the point of a second case: it tests whether the model is consistent on one dish across two photographs.

Four golden-brown triangular fried pastries on a black plate against a dark background, with a small black bowl of green chutney garnished with a coriander leaf. The triangular form and the blistered pastry are unambiguous. Samosa's second case, and a cleaner photograph than the dim restaurant plate in batch 10, which is why both are kept.
